items: Former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte is set to face trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) for three counts of crimes against humanity related to his war on drugs.
The trial will begin on November 30, 2026, where judges will confirm the charges and hear opening statements from the prosecution and victims' representatives.

MANILA, Philippines – A week from now, the trial of former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte before the International Criminal Court (ICC) will mark a new phase in the proceedings over alleged crimes committed during his violent war on drugs.
Duterte faces three counts of crimes against humanity, involving murder and attempted murder allegedly committed in the Philippines between November 1, 2011, and March 16, 2019.
The charges cover killings in Davao City during his time as mayor, the deaths of alleged high-value targets during his presidency, and killings linked to police anti-drug operations in communities.

The ICC Pre-Trial Chamber I unanimously confirmed all three counts on April 23, 2026. In its decision, the chamber said that there “are substantial grounds to believe that Mr. Duterte is criminally responsible for the crimes.” On October 8, it also ruled that Duterte was fit to stand trial.

blocks.caption: TIMELINE: The road to Duterte’s trial at the International Criminal Court

blocks.text: The trial will open on Monday, November 30, before ICC Trial Chamber III. The chamber includes Presiding Judge Joanna Korner, Judge Keebong Paek, and Judge Nicolas Guillou.
During this time, judges will first confirm that Duterte understands the charges against him. They will then ask him whether he admits guilt or pleads not guilty.

The chamber will proceed with the opening statements of the prosecution and the Common Legal Representatives of Victims (CLRV). The defense may also deliver an opening statement if it chooses to do so.
The prosecution has been given six hours for its opening statement, while the victims’ representatives have three hours.

According to a primer of the ICC, the first prosecution witness is scheduled to testify after the opening statements. The court also expects the first five prosecution witnesses to take the stand before the court takes a break starting December 18.
The trial will resume on January 11, 2027.
For the opening days of the trial, the ICC has scheduled four hearing sessions per day.

It is important to note that ICC livestreams will have a 30-minute delay. This means viewers online, outside the courtroom, can expect to start watching the proceedings at 5:30 pm, Philippine time.
The ICC has not announced a fixed daily schedule for the succeeding phases of the trial. The timing and duration of hearings will depend on how the proceedings unfold.
The length of Duterte’s trial has not been determined.
The ICC said trials involving crimes against humanity can take several years, depending on the complexity of the case and challenges that arise during proceedings.

The prosecution is also expected to present its case over several months of hearings following the opening statements. The CLRV may then submit observations, while the defense will have the opportunity to present its case and call witnesses.
The prosecution currently anticipates calling approximately 100 witnesses, according to the ICC.
“The judges are committed to expediting the trial as much as possible,” it added. – Rappler.com
